s: Mainland beach north of Yanbu · the best-known green turtle rookery in Saudi Arabia
te: The beach where turtles keep coming back
se: North of Yanbu, hundreds of green turtles crawl ashore each year to lay their eggs, and their numbers have grown since the 1980s
sa: شمال ينبع تزحف مئات السلاحف الخضراء إلى الشاطئ كل عام لتضع بيضها، وقد ازدادت أعدادها منذ ثمانينيات القرن الماضي
desc: A mainland nesting beach on the Red Sea coast about 70 km north of Yanbu, next to the Yanbu Cement Factory. Annual counts of nesting green turtles (Chelonia mydas) rose from 14–110 females in 1982–1995 to 178 in 2018 and 330 in 2019, and Shimada et al. (2021) estimated an upward trend at the site. Satellite tracking in September–October 2019 (with tagged turtles from Mashabah Island) gave a mean re-nesting interval of 10.8 days and showed nesting success above 0.8 when daytime sand-surface temperature was below 37 °C, falling below 0.4 above 47 °C.
sig: A major and growing green turtle rookery in the Red Sea and a test case for how warming sand may affect nesting.
ex: Shimada et al. (2021); Scott et al. (2022)
disc: 330 nesting females in 2019, up from 14–110 in 1982–1995
Next to a cement factory, yet numbers are rising
Hot sand above 47 °C cuts nesting success
refs: Shimada, T., Meekan, M.G., Baldwin, R., Al-Suwailem, A.M., Clarke, C., Santillan, A.S. & Duarte, C.M. (2021). Distribution and temporal trends in the abundance of nesting sea turtles in the Red Sea. Biological Conservation 261, 109235. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.biocon.2021.109235

Shimada, T., Duarte, C.M., Al-Suwailem, A.M., Tanabe, L.K. & Meekan, M.G. (2021). Satellite tracking reveals nesting patterns, site fidelity, and potential impacts of warming on major green turtle rookeries in the Red Sea. Frontiers in Marine Science 8, 633814. https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2021.633814

Scott et al. (2022). Newly described nesting sites of the green sea turtle (Chelonia mydas) and the hawksbill sea turtle (Eretmochelys imbricata) in the central Red Sea. PeerJ 10, e13408. https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj.13408
Arab News (17 June 2026). Saudi Arabia leads efforts to protect sea turtles. https://www.arabnews.com/node/2647549/saudi-arabia
conf: Coordinates are the Ras Baridi site point published by Scott et al. (2022). The 70 km distance from Yanbu is from Arab News (2026). Timeline starts at the first nesting counts (1982). Arabic name is a careful transliteration.

s: Uninhabited island off Al Wajh · a major green turtle rookery recognised in 2018–2019
se: On a lonely island far from any town, almost two hundred green turtles were found nesting in a single year
sa: على جزيرة نائية بعيدة عن أي مدينة، وُجد قرابة مئتي سلحفاة خضراء تعشّش في عام واحد
desc: Jazirat Mashabah is an uninhabited island in the northern Red Sea, about 65 km from the nearest city, Al Wajh. Surveys counted 113 nesting green turtle (Chelonia mydas) females in 2018 and 179 in 2019, identifying it as a major rookery not previously described. In September–October 2019, 20 turtles were fitted with satellite tags here, and 13 of them nested after tagging. One tracked turtle travelled to Jazirat Al Fawaidah, 84 km to the south-east, but did not nest there.
sig: One of the largest green turtle rookeries in the Red Sea, documented only recently.
disc: 113 nesting females in 2018, 179 in 2019
65 km from Al Wajh, the nearest city
20 turtles satellite-tagged in 2019
refs: Shimada, T., Meekan, M.G., Baldwin, R., Al-Suwailem, A.M., Clarke, C., Santillan, A.S. & Duarte, C.M. (2021). Distribution and temporal trends in the abundance of nesting sea turtles in the Red Sea. Biological Conservation 261, 109235. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.biocon.2021.109235

Shimada, T., Duarte, C.M., Al-Suwailem, A.M., Tanabe, L.K. & Meekan, M.G. (2021). Satellite tracking reveals nesting patterns, site fidelity, and potential impacts of warming on major green turtle rookeries in the Red Sea. Frontiers in Marine Science 8, 633814. https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2021.633814
conf: Coordinates are the two-decimal site point given by Shimada et al. (2021, Frontiers), printed there as 25.65°S, 36.45°E; the S is a typo for N. Precision is about 1 km. The island lies within the Al-Wajh Bank area but is about 35 km west of the existing Al Wajh Lagoon pin and is a distinct turtle rookery. Arabic name is a careful transliteration. Region set to Tabuk (Al Wajh governorate).

s: Mangrove lagoon near Duba · close to the northern limit of mangroves on the Saudi Red Sea coast
dr: Northern limit mapped in the KSLOF Atlas (2012)
el: Northern limit of Avicennia marina near 27°25′N
te: The last mangroves of the north
se: Near Duba grow the most northerly grey mangroves on the Saudi Red Sea coast, where the sea becomes too cool and salty for most
sa: قرب ضباء تنمو أشجار القرم الرمادي الأبعد شمالًا على ساحل البحر الأحمر السعودي
desc: The Khaled bin Sultan Living Oceans Foundation Atlas of Saudi Arabian Red Sea Marine Habitats gives Sharm Zubeir (27°25′N), between Al-Sourah and Sharma just north of Duba, as the northern limit of grey mangrove (Avicennia marina) on the Saudi coast. Al-Hasawi (2022) sampled mangrove trees and sediments at a Duba site at 27°25′38″N, 35°36′06″E, described as an inland lagoon away from human activities, as the northernmost of ten stations between Duba and Al-Birk. The same study cites an estimate of about 135 km² of mangrove forest along the Saudi Red Sea shoreline.
sig: Marks the northern edge of mangrove growth on the Saudi Red Sea coast, a natural limit set by climate.
disc: Northern limit of grey mangrove near 27°25′N
Northernmost of 10 sampled mangrove stations
About 135 km² of mangroves on the Saudi Red Sea coast
refs: Bruckner, A., Rowlands, G., Riegl, B., Purkis, S., Williams, A. & Renaud, P. (2012). Khaled bin Sultan Living Oceans Foundation Atlas of Saudi Arabian Red Sea Marine Habitats. Panoramic Press, Phoenix, AZ. ISBN 978-0-9835611-1-8. https://livingoceansfoundation.org/wp-content/uploads/2014/01/Red-Sea-Atlas-English.pdf

Al-Hasawi, Z.M. (2022). Determination of potentially toxic metals in mangrove trees and associated sediments along Saudi Red Sea coast. Egyptian Journal of Aquatic Biology & Fisheries 26(6), 595–617. https://ejabf.journals.ekb.eg/article_274585_340cbb9e25600b769fbc9803d5aa7666.pdf
conf: Coordinates are the Duba mangrove station of Al-Hasawi (2022), converted from degrees-minutes-seconds. That station's latitude matches the Atlas's Sharm Zubeir limit (27°25′N), but neither source explicitly says they are the same stand, so the record is named for Duba. The 135 km² figure is Al-Hasawi's citation of Almahasheer et al. (2016). Timeline starts at the Atlas (2012). Arabic name is descriptive.

s: Island-sheltered bay near Al-Lith · densest Sooty Falcon population in Saudi Arabia
te: The bay of the Sooty Falcons
se: A shallow bay hidden behind a long island, where mangrove islets shelter falcons, terns and nesting sea turtles
sa: خليج ضحل يحتمي خلف جزيرة طويلة، تؤوي جُزُره المكسوّة بالقرم الصقور والخطاطيف والسلاحف البحرية التي تعشّش فيه
desc: A shallow bay of about 15 × 35 km on the Red Sea coast near Al-Lith, almost enclosed by a long, narrow island and eight smaller islets, where the Asir mountains come close to the sea. Most islets are fringed by Avicennia mangroves and covered in dense Salicornia, and seagrass beds grow in the bay. The site holds the densest Sooty Falcon (Falco concolor) population in Saudi Arabia, at least 50 breeding pairs of Bridled Tern, and breeding hawksbill and green turtles; dugongs also occur. Traditional trapping of migrating falcons between mid-September and mid-November is listed as a threat.
sig: A key Red Sea site for breeding falcons, seabirds and sea turtles and a bottleneck for migrating raptors.
disc: Densest Sooty Falcon population in Saudi Arabia
At least 50 pairs of Bridled Tern
Hawksbill and green turtles breed here
refs: Key Biodiversity Areas Partnership. Qishran Bay (KBA 8277), Saudi Arabia – site factsheet (BirdLife International data; last assessed 1994). https://www.keybiodiversityareas.org/site/factsheet/8277
conf: Coordinates are the KBA central point; the site covers 586 km², so the pin shows only its general position. Timeline starts from the KBA’s last assessment (1994). Arabic name is a careful transliteration. Region set to Makkah (Al-Lith governorate) from the location.

s: Four small islands off Al-Lith · the largest recorded sea turtle nesting site in Saudi waters
dr: Announced as the largest turtle nesting site, November 2024
te: Four sisters full of turtle nests
se: Far out on the Farasan Banks, four little islands hold more than 2,500 nests of green and hawksbill turtles
sa: في عرض ضفاف فرسان، تحتضن أربع جزر صغيرة أكثر من 2,500 عش للسلاحف الخضراء وصقرية المنقار
desc: Marmar, Dahreb, Malathu and Jadir are four small islands of the Farasan Banks, about 50 km off Al-Lith, lying within about 7 km of Jadir. In November 2024 the General Organization for the Conservation of Coral Reefs and Marine Turtles in the Red Sea (SHAMS) announced that more than 2,500 turtle nests had been recorded there, the largest recorded sea turtle nesting site in Saudi waters. Both green turtles and critically endangered hawksbills nest on the islands. Satellite tags fitted to green turtles on Jadir in 2021 recorded further nesting attempts, most of them on Jadir itself.
sig: The largest documented sea turtle nesting site in the Saudi Red Sea, important for both green and hawksbill turtles.
disc: More than 2,500 turtle nests
Green and hawksbill turtles both nest
Four islands about 50 km offshore
refs: Tanabe, L.K., Cochran, J.E.M. & Berumen, M.L. (2023). Inter-nesting, migration, and foraging behaviors of green turtles (Chelonia mydas) in the central-southern Red Sea. Scientific Reports 13, 11222. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-023-37942-z

Scott et al. (2022). Newly described nesting sites of the green sea turtle (Chelonia mydas) and the hawksbill sea turtle (Eretmochelys imbricata) in the central Red Sea. PeerJ 10, e13408. https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj.13408
Arab News (2 November 2024). Saudi foundation discovers largest recorded sea turtle nesting site in Red Sea. https://www.arabnews.pk/node/2577799
conf: Pin is Jadir Island, the coordinate published by Tanabe et al. (2023); Scott et al. (2022) give Mar Mar at 19.83576°N, 39.92635°E. The 7 km spacing is from the Tanabe et al. text (their figure caption says 10 km). The nest total is a press-release figure and has not been seen in a peer-reviewed table. Arabic name «جزر الأخوات الأربع» is a translation of the English name. Region set to Makkah (offshore of Al-Lith).

s: Narrow intertidal mudflat in Jazan city · over 20,000 wintering waterbirds counted
te: A city shore full of birds
se: Right beside Jazan city, a thin strip of tidal mud feeds thousands of wading birds in winter
sa: بجوار مدينة جازان مباشرة، يُطعم شريط رفيع من الطين المدّي آلاف الطيور الخوّاضة في الشتاء
desc: A narrow strip of intertidal mudflats about 4 km long and 500 m wide, running from Jizan Port to the northern edge of Jizan city. Sewage outflow from the city enriches the flats, which were once fringed by mangroves that have since been lost to land reclamation. Counts reached 20,053 waterbirds in January 1992, an unusually cold winter, and 10,000–15,000 in December 1992. Part of the site was proposed as a Special Nature Reserve in the NCWCD System Plan for Protected Areas.
sig: Shows how a small urban mudflat can support internationally important numbers of waterbirds.
disc: About 4 km long and 500 m wide
20,053 waterbirds in January 1992
Former mangroves lost to reclamation
refs: Key Biodiversity Areas Partnership. Jizan Bay (KBA 8289), Saudi Arabia – site factsheet (BirdLife International data; last assessed 1994). https://www.keybiodiversityareas.org/site/factsheet/8289
conf: Coordinates are the KBA central point. Waterbird counts date from 1992 and may not reflect present numbers. Timeline starts from the KBA’s last assessment (1994).

s: Semi-enclosed bay at Baish, Jazan · mangrove seedlings, seagrass and 29 waterbird species studied
ta: شتلات القرم في مواجهة العواصف الرملية
se: In a hot, salty bay at Baish, scientists watched young mangroves fight sandstorms while gulls and plovers fed on the seagrass
sa: في خليج حار شديد الملوحة في بيش، تابع العلماء شتلات القرم وهي تقاوم العواصف الرملية، بينما تتغذّى النوارس والزقزاق بين الأعشاب البحرية
desc: A semi-enclosed bay at Baish on the southern Saudi Red Sea coast, inside the Jazan City for Primary and Downstream Industries, with grey mangrove (Avicennia marina) and seagrass. Between April and July 2017, 53 mangrove seedlings were tracked across four tidal zones; only three (5.6%) survived, a loss attributed mainly to burial by sandstorms, while seawater reached 35–37 °C and salinity 46.9–53.01. Bird counts at three stations recorded 29 species from 14 families and 514 individuals, led by Common Gull (202) and Kentish Plover (51), with most birds at the station next to the mangroves.
sig: A natural laboratory for how mangroves and seagrass survive extreme heat, salinity and dust at the southern Red Sea.
disc: Only 3 of 53 seedlings survived the summer
Seawater 35–37 °C, salinity up to 53
29 bird species, 514 birds counted
refs: Abrogueña, J.B.R., Anton, A., Woo, S.P., Baptista, M., Duarte, C.M., Hussain, S.A., Shoeb, M. & Qurban, M. (2022). The impact of inundation and sandstorms on the growth and survival of the mangrove Avicennia marina seedlings in the southern Red Sea. Scientia Marina 86(3), e041. https://doi.org/10.3989/scimar.05277.041

Abrogueña, J.B.R., Tanita, I., Doyle, A.M., Roje-Busatto, R., Maquirang, J.R.H., Manokaran, S., Imam, K., Al-Johani, T. & Woo, S.P. (2025). Seagrass and mangroves as water-associated bird habitat in the southern Red Sea coasts of Saudi Arabia. Marine Ornithology 53(1), 87–98. https://www.marineornithology.org/PDF/53_1/53_1_87-98.pdf
conf: Coordinates are the site centre published by Abrogueña et al. (2022); the 2025 bird stations lie within about 2 km (17.32019–17.3587°N, 42.30896–42.32896°E). The 2025 paper’s Discussion says 15 species, conflicting with 29 in its Results; 29 is used. Timeline starts at the 2017 fieldwork. Arabic name is descriptive.

s: Shallow seagrass bay on the Arabian Gulf · about 58,000 wintering waterbirds and feeding dugongs and turtles
te: The seagrass meadow of the Gulf
se: A clear, shallow bay where seagrass feeds dugongs and green turtles and tens of thousands of birds spend the winter
sa: خليج صافٍ ضحل تغذّي أعشابه البحرية الأطوم والسلاحف الخضراء، ويقضي فيه عشرات الآلاف من الطيور فصل الشتاء
desc: A clear, shallow bay on the Saudi coast of the Arabian Gulf around Tarut Island, with mostly sandy bottoms and extensive seagrass beds. Its intertidal zone is among the richest in the Saudi sector of the Arabian Gulf, with broad sand-mud and mud flats once fringed by mangrove and saltmarsh, much of which has been lost to land reclamation. About 58,000 waterbirds wintered here in 1991/92 and more than 20,000 were present in April–May 1991, with six wintering Greater Spotted Eagles and 11 Ospreys. The bay is an important feeding area for green turtles, supports dugongs and serves as a nursery for shrimp and fish.
sig: One of the most productive seagrass and mudflat systems on the Saudi Arabian Gulf coast.
disc: About 58,000 wintering waterbirds
Feeding ground for green turtles and dugongs
Nursery for shrimp and fish
refs: Key Biodiversity Areas Partnership. Tarut Bay (KBA 8262), Saudi Arabia – site factsheet (BirdLife International data; last assessed 1994). https://www.keybiodiversityareas.org/site/factsheet/8262
conf: Coordinates are the KBA central point; it lies about 4 km from the existing Tarout Island (archaeological) pin but records the bay’s ecology, not the island’s archaeology. Bird counts date from 1991–1992. Timeline starts from the KBA’s last assessment (1994).
